aAbout: MarineTraffic (founded 2007) is the default ship-tracking platform: real-time vessel positions from thousands of shore AIS receivers, live ETAs and arrival/departure schedules for 4,000+ ports, vessel particulars and photos, port-call logs and animated voyage playback. The free tier opens the map but reserves menus and features for registered users; paid plans scale from a 10-vessel Basic list up to Enterprise fleets of 2,000 vessels with five years of history. Its parent company also sells risk, compliance and port-intelligence products built on the same data.
aStrengths: MarineTraffic is the maritime-intelligence leader: 4,000+ port schedules with live ETAs, animated historical playback (up to five years of history on Enterprise), port-call logs, vessel ownership and dimensions, 48-hour wind forecasts, fleet management, a voyage planner and a mature commercial API. For compliance analysts, sanctions researchers, port professionals and fleet operators, its institutional depth is in a different league.
bAbout: VesselFinder tracks ships worldwide through 7,000+ terrestrial AIS data sources, with satellite AIS layered on top for open-ocean coverage (it says 90% of satellite positions arrive within an hour). The site pairs positions with vessel photos, port data, weather overlays and a distance tool. Its plans are published in plain dollars and undercut the market leader at every tier, and its subscriptions do not renew automatically. API access and historical data are sold separately.
bStrengths: VesselFinder's edge is honest, budget maritime tracking: affordable satellite AIS covering the open oceans where terrestrial receivers can't reach, a practical single-ship satellite pass for occasional needs, vessel photos and particulars, and plans that undercut the big rival at every level — Basic is $12 for a whole year. For port agents, cargo superintendents and individual surveyors who need affordable fleet watching, it is the value play in ship tracking.
betterAnswer: MarineTraffic is better for professional depth — port schedules, ETAs, playback, history and compliance-grade data. VesselFinder is better value for straightforward tracking — cheaper plans, cheaper satellite coverage, no automatic renewal. Casual viewers checking one ship are served by either free tier; the paid decision is really about whether you need MarineTraffic's port and history machinery.

faqs.a: On land, both are strong — they aggregate thousands of terrestrial AIS receivers. Offshore, coverage depends on satellite AIS: MarineTraffic includes it from its Essential plan (one vessel at a time), while VesselFinder's Satellite plan covers an unlimited fleet. In dense coastal waters the two are broadly comparable.
faqs.q: Which has better coverage, MarineTraffic or VesselFinder?

faqs.a: MarineTraffic's Basic plan is £10 per user per month (10 vessels, 100 notifications/month); Essential is £100 per user per month and adds 7-day history plus satellite positions for one vessel at a time; Enterprise is quoted and reaches 2,000 vessels with 5-year history.

Free (10 ships, 1-day history), Basic $4/month or $12/year (20 ships, 3-day history), Premium $34/month or $179/year (500 ships, 7-day history) and Satellite $139/month or $1,399/year (2,000 ships, 90-day history, satellite AIS). MarineTraffic's free tier lets you view the live map, but menus and features require registration. VesselFinder's free tier is functional without paying, with ad interruptions and small limits (10 ships, 1-day history).
faqs.q: Which is better for free ship tracking?

faqs.a: WorldEye shows live ship positions free on its 3D globe — no registration — together with flights, satellites, weather and 74,229 cameras. For port schedules, playback and history, MarineTraffic and VesselFinder remain the specialists.
faqs.q: Is there a free ship tracker with no registration?

faqs.a: For professional work, MarineTraffic is the standard — port schedules with live ETAs, historical playback, fleet tools and a commercial API. For everyday tracking on a budget, VesselFinder is the value pick, with an honest free tier and affordable satellite AIS for open-ocean coverage. Both run on AIS data, so the real differences are coverage depth, history and port tooling. WorldEye's globe includes a ship layer alongside its cameras and flights, but its AIS feed is not currently returning live vessel positions — for ship tracking today, the two specialists above are the picks.

intro: MarineTraffic and VesselFinder answer the same question — where is that ship? — at very different prices. MarineTraffic is the industry's default: the biggest receiver network reputation, 4,000+ ports with live ETAs, deep history and a compliance business built on top. VesselFinder is the challenger that publishes simple dollar pricing and undercuts it at every tier, including satellite coverage of the open ocean. If you track ships for work or for love, this is the comparison that decides your subscription.

verdictA: Choose MarineTraffic if ships are your job — port operations, fleet management, journalism or compliance — and you need schedules, ETAs, playback and years of history more than you need a low price.
verdictB: Choose VesselFinder if you track a fleet or a few favourite ships on a budget, want satellite ocean coverage without enterprise pricing, and prefer subscriptions that never renew behind your back.
worldEye: For casual watching, WorldEye shows live ships free on a 3D globe — no registration at all — in the same view as live flights, satellites, weather, earthquakes, wildfires and 74,229 public cameras. It has neither MarineTraffic's port machinery nor VesselFinder's satellite plans; it's the free, everything-at-once picture. An optional Pro tier ($7.99/week, $13.99/month or $74.99/year) adds the OSINT toolkit and maritime intel feeds.
